title: The created body of Christ shown by his passion and resurrection
english: If anyone says that the body of Christ is uncreated, and does not confess that the uncreated God the Word himself displayed his incarnation from created humanity and became man as it is written, let him be anathema. For how can a body be called uncreated? What is uncreated is also incapable of suffering, and can be neither wounded nor touched. But Christ, rising from the dead, showed the disciples the marks of the nails and the wound made by the lance, and his body able to be touched, and he entered through closed doors. He did this to display both the works of his divinity and the reality of his body: although he was otherwise God, he was recognized as man; and although he was truly man, God was nevertheless demonstrated from his own works.
notes_covered: Cap. I anathema against calling Christ's body uncreated
Explication: uncreated = impassible/intangible vs risen body handled behind shut doors
Tip scope: Capita I-II only; remaining ten anathemas later

added_allusions.reason: risen body handled; shut doors; nails and spear

translator_notes: Locked from Vossius 1684 Latin column; Greek column OCR too damaged to serve as copy-text.
ANF 6 Crombie exists and was used only as a sense check, not as the reading English.
OCR joins on clavorum/lancea/palpandum disclosed; sense checked against the facing column and the John 20 scene.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. I (anathema + interpretatio)
orientation: Gregory opens his treatise by anathematizing anyone who says Christ's body is uncreated, then argues that the risen Christ's wounds and touchable body prove it was created.

title: The flesh is not consubstantial with the divinity
english: If anyone says that the flesh of Christ is consubstantial with the divinity, and does not confess that he himself was in the form of God and was God before the ages, and that he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, as it is written, let him be anathema. For how can flesh that exists after time be called consubstantial with the sempiternal divinity? What is consubstantial is what is the same in nature and in sempiternity, without change.
notes_covered: Cap. II anathema against homoousion of flesh with divinity
Explication: post-temporal flesh cannot share the Godhead's everlasting sameness

added_allusions.reason: in the form of God; emptied himself; form of a servant

translator_notes: Homoousion kept as the Latin column's Greek loanword, then glossed consubstantial.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. II (anathema + interpretatio)
orientation: Gregory is closing his treatise with a final anathema against saying Christ's flesh is consubstantial with the divinity.
